title: What is known about 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LB_0RD0RF_0RD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LB_0RD0RF_0RD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it halts. Busycoq pull request 93 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-17) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer has not yet reviewed it. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

What this repository found on its own. A bouncer over the 9-cell word 110101010 on the left; the slow right side is a list of blocks 1^(6j+1) 00, mostly sorted by length, through which waves of rewriting pass. Same mechanism as 1RB1RE_1RC0RF_0LD---_1LE1LD_1RA0LB_0RE0RF (and probably the part03 twin).
Lean proves no halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps (the first 10,000 by the kernel alone), 8 shift rules of the sweeps; the rest of the description below is observation of the run, marked as such.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 37,151 cells have been visited and 22,314 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.503). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.162).

claims.title: 8 shift rules of the sweeps
claims.text: For every n and every tape around: A crosses 110101010 rightward writing 001111111, C crosses it leftward writing 111011101 (eight proved rules over its rotations). Each is a theorem steps (s·n) … = some … found and proved by tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py.

claims.title: Where a halt can happen (closed tape language, 5-cell windows)
claims.text: The closure search of bbtools.ctl with windows of 5 cells is closed but allows halts; the halting abstract configurations constrain the neighbourhood of a halt: a halt (F reading 1) needs 00110 or 00111 to the left; any right side starting with 1. A Python check, not a Lean certificate (the Lean library only has the right-edge and no-halt corollaries, which do not apply).

claims.title: No halt in the first 6.64×10<sup>13</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 6.64×1013 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 6 checkpoints, the last at 1.00×1010 steps. Of these steps, the part after the last checkpoint rests on the simulator alone, including 8,016 trip-level jumps: a jump applies many identical round trips at once after seeing the same tape shape recur with constant count changes, which is validated against direct simulation but not proved.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. F reading 1 halts. The 5-cell closed language allows that with 0011x on the left and any right window starting with 1.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tape and head as 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LE_1LC0RF_0RD--- at every one of the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps (the tables differ). The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 1 other holdout (listed on the explainer page).

explainer.lede: It halts. One side of the tape is a bouncer; the other is a sorted list of runs of 1s of lengths 6j+1 that works like a counter, each pass halving the runs of one length and moving them up a length. Long after any simulation could follow, the counter's leftovers line up into the pattern that stops it: busycoq pull request 93 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind proves it in Rocq.

No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: A counter of digit rows, run by a proved engine
html: The proof is busycoq pull request 93 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind. We compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch in about 9 minutes; it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions halt prints “Closed under the global context”). It does not find a formula for the run. It builds a fast simulator, the engine, proves in Coq that every step of the engine is a true statement about the machine, and then lets the engine run the machine from the blank tape until it halts.

A copy of the table. The proof first reflects the tape, so that left and right swap, and renames the states: this machine's A, B, C, D become C, D, A, B. That gives the table 1RB1RA_1LC0RD_1LD1LB_1RA0LE_0LB0LF_0LB--- started in state C. Coq checks transition by transition that the two runs are the same up to this change, so a halt of one is a halt of the other. From here on, directions and state names are those of that table. Call this table T3. Changed in F0 it becomes T4, the table of three other holdouts (started in B, C and D). This repository adapted the engine to T4 and proved the B and C starts halting, and also a fourth holdout that reduces to T4 started in A.

Digits and three moments. Write wn for the word w written n times. The proof's main word is the digit D n = 1 (11)n 00: a run of 2n+1 ones followed by two blanks. Call n its level. The blocks 1^(6j+1) 00 of the sections below are the digits D 3j, seen reflected. Most of the tape is a long sequence of digits, mostly in rows of equal ones, the highest levels towards the left and the lowest at the right end. Near the left end, where the head turns, lie a few other kinds of word, among them blocks (10)b and (111)k. The proof watches the head at three kinds of moment: CfgR, state A at the word 0100, heading right over the digits; CfgL, state B heading left with a 1 just behind it; and CfgJ, state C heading left with 100 just behind it and a +1 to deliver.

Macro rules. About twenty rules say how the machine gets from one such moment to the next, for every level and every surrounding tape. Heading right, the head turns each digit D n it crosses into S n = 1 (01)n+1, a word of the same length. Heading left in CfgL it turns S n back into D n; in CfgJ it turns it into D (n+1), which is how a +1 is delivered. At the blank end of the tape the head writes two new digits D 0 and turns back. On the left, each 111 of a block (111)k is used up by one turn, so the block is a timer that allows k more round trips. And a round trip that finds two digits D 0 side by side merges them: 10 D0 D0 becomes D2 10, and the digit before them gets a +1; over a row, 2k digits D 0 become about k digits D 3. Rows of higher digits are merged in pairs in the same way, through a longer detour over the left part.

A counter. Together these rules make the digits a counter. Its places are the levels 0, 3, 6, …, and the number of digits in a row is the value at that place. Each pass halves a row and carries it one place up, while fresh digits D 0 keep arriving at the right end. This is binary counting with rows instead of bits, so a row of n digits lasts about log2 n passes. The halving is not exact: a row with an odd count leaves a digit over, and the proof has rules for these leftovers (it calls them defects). Where the leftovers end up depends on the parities of huge counts, and no formula for them is known. That is why the community calls such a machine a chaotic Bell.

The engine. The engine is a program written in Coq. It stores the tape compactly: the left part as a list of words with repeat counts, the digits as a list of pairs (level, how many in a row), all numbers in binary. In one engine step it looks at the tape near the head, picks the rule that applies, often a whole batch of them (k round trips at once, with k found by a division), and writes down the result. Where no rule fits, it makes single machine steps. One theorem, proved for every possible compact tape, says that each engine step is correct: the machine really goes from the tape before to the tape after, and when the engine reports a halt, the machine really halts.

How it stops. In this machine's own terms it halts only when state B reads a 1 and the two cells to its right are 1 too: B1 and E1 then put F on a 1. Nothing in the proof predicts when the leftovers will set this up; the engine simply runs until they do. Coq's virtual machine (vm_compute) evaluates the engine from the blank tape with a budget of 222 = 4,194,304 steps, and it stops after 2,452,242 of them, when the newest row holds about 10420 digits D 0, far beyond any direct simulation. So the computer checks one long but finite computation. What holds for all sizes (the rules, the batches, the correctness of every engine step) is proved by symbolic reasoning in Coq.

sections.heading: What the machine does: bouncer with a sorted list of blocks 1^(6j+1)
html: Left of the start the tape is (110 10 10 10) repeated (tokens b a^3 with b=110, a=10), the background of a bouncer growing like √t.

Right of it, on the slow side (395 cells right of the start after 109 steps, exponent about 0.16), the tape is a list of blocks of 1s separated by 00. The settled blocks have lengths 6j + 1 and are sorted: … 1^25 0^2 1^25 0^2 1^29 0^2 1^31 0^2 … 1^31 0^2 1^35 0^2 1^37 … 1^41 0^2 1^43 … 1^47 0^2 1^49 0^2 1^49 0^2 1^9 0^2 1 0^2 1 0^2 1^59 0 1 0^2 1^5 0^2 1^11 0^2 1^2 B>0 (step 246,254,433). Blocks of length 6j + 5 (29, 35, 41, 47, 53) sit at the boundaries between groups, and the last few blocks near the right end are in the middle of being rewritten.

Over time the groups move up: near the right end the 1^25 group is gone by step 6·108 and the visible list runs from 1^31 to 1^63 at 9.5·108. It looks like a sorted counter whose digits are block lengths, incremented by 6 when a wave passes; we had not written its rule. The proof has it: see How the proof works.

sections.heading: What a halt would require
html: F reading 1 halts. The 5-cell closed language allows that with 0011x on the left and any right window starting with 1.

It happens: state B reads 1 1 1 (B1 and E1 put F on a 1) after 2,452,242 steps of the proved engine of busycoq pull request 93, when the newest row of the counter holds about 10420 digits D 0, single 1s between blanks.

sections.heading: What is proved, and what is not
html:
• Sweeps (lean/Sweeps.lean, kernel): A crosses 110101010 rightward writing 001111111, C crosses it leftward writing 111011101 (eight proved rules over its rotations); for every number of copies and every tape around.
  • Bounded run (lean/Blank.lean): no halt in 107 steps (native), 10,000 (kernel); the halting transition is the only way to stop.
Everything else on this page is observation of the simulated run (heuristic). Nothing proved in this repository decides halting; the outside proof does.

sections.heading: What is left
html: Halting is settled by the outside proof, whose engine contains the rule of one visit of the head to the right wall that this page had planned to write. Still open here: the comparison with 1RB1RE_1RC0RF_0LD---_1LE1LD_1RA0LB_0RE0RF, which agrees with this machine on the first records and then diverges, and is still an open holdout.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.503). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.162).
After 109 steps the tape spans 37,151 cells (26,993 left of the start, 395 right), with a density of 1s of 0.601.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same run as 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LE_1LC0RF_0RD--- (observed, not proved). At every one of the first 107 steps from blank tape the two machines have the same tape and the head on the same cell. Their tables differ, and no renaming of the states turns one into the other. While they run, the states pair up as A–A, B–B, B–E, C–C, D–D, E–E, E–F, F–F (this machine first), which is not one to one. Transitions not used in these steps: this machine never uses F1 and the other never uses F1. Lean proves (lean/Twin.lean here, lock_or_break, not_halts_of_noBreak) that the two runs have the same tape, the same head position and paired states up to the first break, a configuration where the paired states act differently, and that neither machine halts if no break ever comes. A halt of either machine is itself a break, and the halting transitions of the two do not correspond, so the two are not known to halt together.

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

  • 1RB1RE_1RC0RF_0LD---_1LE1LD_1RA0LB_0RE0RF: 8,004,077 configurations, the last at step 8,004,076 here and step 10,000,000 there
